items.jurisdiction_note: CDC Standard Precautions ≈ Canadian Routine Practices for localized coverable shingles in immunocompetent hosts.
items.topic: Localized herpes zoster (immunocompetent, coverable) — Standard/Routine Practices until lesions dry and crusted
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: An immunocompetent older adult has localized herpes zoster (shingles) on the trunk; lesions can be completely covered with a dressing. Which infection-control approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Standard Precautions (Routine Practices) with lesions covered until dry and crusted
Airborne and Contact Precautions in a negative-pressure room for the entire admission regardless of immune status
Droplet Precautions only for 24 hours after the first vesicle appears
No precautions are needed even if lesions are uncovered and draining

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: localized zoster in immunocompetent hosts with containable/coverable lesions → Standard Precautions until lesions dry and crusted. PHO: localized shingles require Routine Practices (vs airborne+contact for disseminated).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Airborne + Contact is for disseminated disease or localized disease in immunocompromised hosts until dissemination is ruled out.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Zoster is not managed with Droplet-only precautions for 24 hours.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Covering lesions and Standard/Routine Practices are required until crusted; uncovered draining lesions increase transmission risk.

rationales.R4: Not indicated. Lesions should be covered to reduce transmission.
rationales.R5: Indicated. CDC: disseminated (any patient) or localized immunocompromised until dissemination ruled out → Airborne + Contact.

items.topic: Multidose vials — dedicate to a single patient when possible; new sterile needle/syringe each entry
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Which practice best reduces infection risk when using a multidose medication vial?

options.text: Dedicate the multidose vial to a single patient when possible and use a new sterile needle and syringe for every entry
Leave a needle in the vial septum between doses so the vial stays 'open' for faster access
Reuse the same syringe for several patients if only the needle is changed
Carry one multidose vial from room to room and enter it with previously used syringes

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: dedicate multidose vials to a single patient whenever possible; new sterile syringe/needle each patient. OpenStax: dedicate to single patient when possible; new needles/syringes every injection; do not leave needles in vials.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC/OpenStax: do not leave a needle in the septum (contamination pathway).
rationales.C: Incorrect. CDC: never reuse a syringe for more than one patient even if the needle is changed.
rationales.D: Incorrect. If a multidose vial enters a patient treatment area it must be single-patient only; never enter with used syringes.

items.topic: Occupational blood exposure — wash, report, start HIV PEP as soon as possible (within 72 hours)
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick with a hollow-bore needle used on a client with known HIV infection. After washing the site with soap and water, which next action is the priority?

options.text: Report the exposure immediately and seek urgent evaluation so HIV PEP can start as soon as possible (within 72 hours)
Wait 1 week to see if a rash develops before reporting
Squeeze the puncture site forcefully to 'bleed out' the virus and skip occupational health
Delay care until the source client's full genotype results return next month

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: wash skin after contact; report and get medical care right away; PEP must start within 72 hours; sooner is better. Merck: start PEP as soon after exposure as possible; ideally within 24–36 hours and no later than 72 hours.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Delay beyond the urgent window reduces PEP effectiveness.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Do not rely on squeezing; report and follow exposure protocol.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Do not delay PEP while awaiting non-urgent source details (CDC/Merck emphasize prompt start).

items.topic: Pregnancy Listeria prevention — avoid unheated deli meats and unpasteurized soft cheeses
items.stem: Which teaching point best reduces Listeria risk in pregnancy?

options.text: Avoid unheated deli meats/cold cuts and cheeses made with unpasteurized milk; choose safer heated or pasteurized options
Eat only raw sprouts and refrigerated pâté because they are safest in pregnancy
Listeria cannot affect pregnancy, so no dietary changes are needed
Unpasteurized soft cheeses are preferred over pasteurized hard cheeses

rationales.A: Correct. CDC safer choices: reheat deli meats; avoid unpasteurized milk cheeses. PHAC: higher-risk foods include non-dried deli meats, soft/semi-soft cheeses, unpasteurized milk; pregnant people are high risk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. CDC lists raw sprouts and refrigerated pâté among foods to avoid/choose safer alternatives.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Pregnancy is a high-risk group; infection can harm the fetus/newborn (PHAC).
rationales.D: Incorrect. Unpasteurized soft cheeses are higher risk; pasteurized hard cheeses are safer choices.

items.jurisdiction_note: CDC prefers early 27–36 weeks; NACI ideally 27–32 weeks; both recommend Tdap in every pregnancy.
items.topic: Tdap in every pregnancy to protect the newborn from pertussis
items.stem: A pregnant client asks whether Tdap is needed this pregnancy after receiving Tdap 2 years ago. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Yes — Tdap is recommended during every pregnancy (ideally in the third trimester) to protect the newborn from pertussis
No — one lifetime Tdap dose means no further doses are ever given in pregnancy
Tdap is contraindicated in all pregnancies and must wait until the child is age 5
Only live-virus Tdap is used, and it must be given in the first trimester exclusively

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: Tdap during each pregnancy irrespective of prior history; preferably early 27–36 weeks. NACI: Tdap every pregnancy irrespective of history; ideally 27–32 weeks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prior Tdap does not remove the every-pregnancy recommendation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Tdap in pregnancy is recommended and considered safe in cited guidance.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Tdap is not a live-virus vaccine; timing is third-trimester focused, not first-trimester exclusive.

items.topic: Medication reconciliation at care transitions — compare complete home list to orders
items.stem: Which action best describes medication reconciliation at a care transition?

options.text: Create/verify a complete current medication list (including OTCs) and compare it with new orders to find and resolve discrepancies
Skip home medications and chart only whatever is easiest to remember from shift report
Reconcile only brand-name drugs and ignore vitamins, supplements, and OTC products
Perform reconciliation solely at annual wellness visits, never at admission or discharge

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: identify/verify accurate list (name, dose, frequency, route, why) including OTCs/vitamins/supplements; compare to provider list at any transition. AHRQ MATCH: single shared medication list as one source of truth for ordering/reconciliation across disciplines.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Incomplete lists drive transition errors.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Reconciliation is required at admission, transfer, discharge, and related transitions.
